bill.title: To amend the Plant Protection Act to establish a fund for spotted wing drosophila research and mitigation.
bill.latestActionText: Referred to the House Committee on Agriculture.

industries.rationale: The bill directly addresses an invasive pest that damages fruit crops, affecting farmers and fruit producers who would benefit from research and mitigation programs.

bill.plainSummary: This bill would amend the Plant Protection Act to create a dedicated fund for research and mitigation efforts targeting the spotted wing drosophila, an invasive fruit fly pest. The fund would support scientific studies and control measures for this agricultural pest. The bill does not specify the funding amount or source in the title or summary provided.

bill.title: Providing for congressional disapproval under chapter 8 of title 5, United States Code, of the rule submitted by the United States Fish and Wildlife Service relating to "Endangered and Threatened Wildlife and Plants; Endangered Species Status for the San Francisco Bay-Delta Distinct Population Segment of the Longfin Smelt".

industries.rationale: Endangered species protections in the Bay-Delta region directly affect water allocation for agricultural irrigation in California's Central Valley.
Water management and hydroelectric operations in the Bay-Delta system face regulatory constraints when species are listed as endangered.
Water utilities and water districts must comply with endangered species protections that affect pumping, diversion, and discharge operations in the Bay-Delta.
Development projects near Bay-Delta waterways face additional permitting requirements and habitat mitigation when endangered species are present.

bill.plainSummary: This resolution would overturn a federal rule that listed a specific population of longfin smelt fish in the San Francisco Bay-Delta region as endangered. If passed, the fish would lose protections under the Endangered Species Act that were granted in July 2024. The resolution uses a congressional review process that allows lawmakers to nullify recently issued federal regulations.

plain.whoItTouches: People who keep animals, and people who work with them.

bill.title: SOAR Act of 2025
bill.latestActionText: Referred to the Committee on Energy and Commerce, and in addition to the Committee on Ways and Means, for a period to be subsequently determined by the Speaker, in each case for consideration of such provisions as fall within the jurisdiction of the committee concerned.

industries.rationale: Medical equipment suppliers providing oxygen equipment and related supplies would face new payment methods and regulatory requirements.
Respiratory therapists and providers prescribing oxygen would see new coverage and payment structures under Medicare.
Medicare payment changes for oxygen services could affect supplemental insurance coverage and coordination of benefits.

bill.plainSummary: This bill changes how Medicare pays for supplemental oxygen equipment and services. Instead of using a competitive bidding system, it would establish separate payments that adjust for inflation. It would also formally cover services provided by respiratory therapists, require a standardized electronic prescription form, and give patients specific rights such as choosing their own oxygen supplier.

plain.whoItTouches: Anyone who sees a doctor or pays for care.

bill.title: Accelerating Access to Critical Therapies for ALS Reauthorization Act of 2026
bill.latestActionText: Received in the Senate. Read twice. Placed on Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders. Calendar No. 466.
subjects: Department of Health and Human Services

industries.rationale: The bill directly funds research grants and regulatory pathways for development of drugs and therapies targeting ALS and neurodegenerative diseases.
Providers treating ALS patients may see changes in available investigational therapies and clinical trial access, though the bill focuses primarily on research and regulatory processes.

bill.plainSummary: This bill extends funding through fiscal year 2031 for federal programs that support research and development of treatments for ALS (Lou Gehrig's disease) and similar neurodegenerative diseases. It requires the National Institutes of Health to track safety data on experimental drugs and mandates that the Food and Drug Administration publish a five-year plan describing how it will help develop and approve therapies for these rare diseases. The bill also continues a public-private partnership between federal agencies and outside organizations working on neurodegenerative disease treatments.

plain.whoItTouches: People with an illness that is still being studied. Anyone who uses the internet.

It covers the House of Representatives, Capitol Police, Congressional Budget Office, Architect of the Capitol, Library of Congress, Government Publishing Office, Government Accountability Office, and several smaller congressional offices and joint committees. The bill also establishes rules and restrictions on how these funds may be used.

bill.title: Healthy H2O Act
bill.latestActionText: Referred to the House Committee on Agriculture.

industries.rationale: The bill directly funds water quality testing and contamination reduction, creating new revenue opportunities for water treatment and testing service providers.
Grant-funded water quality improvements in rural homes and facilities would likely require installation of filtration systems and infrastructure work.
The program is administered by USDA and targets rural areas, which may include agricultural operations, though the bill focuses on residential and childcare facilities.

bill.plainSummary: This bill would create a new grant program run by the Department of Agriculture to help people in rural areas improve their drinking water quality. Grants would go to homeowners, renters, and childcare facilities that have tested positive for health contaminants in their water, as well as to nonprofit organizations that help people test their water and reduce contamination.

plain.whoItTouches: People living near whatever is being regulated.

bill.title: Supporting Apprenticeship Colleges Act of 2025
bill.latestActionText: Referred to the House Committee on Education and Workforce.

industries.rationale: The bill provides federal grants directly to institutions of higher education that sponsor apprenticeship programs.
The bill specifically targets construction-oriented registered apprenticeship programs and would fund outreach to construction businesses.
The bill specifically targets manufacturing-oriented registered apprenticeship programs and would fund outreach to manufacturing businesses.

bill.plainSummary: This bill would direct the Department of Education to award grants to colleges and universities that run registered apprenticeship programs in construction and manufacturing. The grants would help these institutions expand outreach to high schools and local businesses, and provide advising and support services to students enrolled in the apprenticeship programs.

plain.whoItTouches: Students, teachers, and the families paying for it.

bill.title: SEED Act
bill.latestActionText: Cloture motion on the motion to proceed to the measure presented in Senate. (CR S4253)

industries.rationale: The bill directly affects early childhood education providers by changing the tax treatment of their employees' expenses.

bill.plainSummary: This bill would allow early childhood educators (pre-kindergarten teachers and staff) to claim the same federal tax deduction for unreimbursed classroom and professional development expenses that is currently available only to kindergarten through grade 12 educators. The deduction is capped at $300 in 2025 and adjusts annually for inflation. It would reduce taxable income for eligible early childhood educators who pay out-of-pocket for supplies and training.

plain.whoItTouches: Anyone who files a tax return. Anyone who pays federal tax.

disclaimer: This tool places two public records next to each other: who donated to a member of Congress, and what that member legislated on. Any overlap you see is a correlation, not causation. It is not evidence of a quid pro quo, of influence, or of wrongdoing. Legislators routinely receive support from industries in their district for the same reason they legislate on them: those industries are there.
